elements.id-string-3: Depth completion is the task of recovering dense depth maps from sparse ones, usually with the help of color images.
elements.id-string-4: Existing image-guided methods perform well on daytime depth perception self-driving benchmarks, but struggle in nighttime scenarios with \textbf{poor visibility} and \textbf{complex illumination}.
elements.id-string-5: To address these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective framework called LDCNet.
elements.id-string-6: Our key idea is to use \emph{Recurrent Inter-Convolution Differencing} (RICD) and \emph{Illumination-Affinitive Intra-Convolution Differencing} (IAICD) to enhance the nighttime color images and reduce the negative effects of the varying illumination, respectively.
elements.id-string-7: RICD explicitly estimates global illumination by differencing two convolutions with different kernels, treating the small-kernel-convolution feature as the center of the large-kernel-convolution feature in a new perspective.
elements.id-string-8: IAICD softly alleviates local relative light intensity by differencing a single convolution, where the center is dynamically aggregated based on neighboring pixels and the estimated illumination map in RICD.
elements.id-string-9: On both nighttime depth completion and depth estimation tasks, extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our LDCNet, reaching the state of the art.
elements.id-string-12: Depth completion aims to predict dense depth maps from sparse ones and the corresponding color images.
elements.id-string-13: It is an essential task in computer vision and has been widely used in various applications, such as augmented reality \cite{dey2012tablet,ma2018self}, 3D scene reconstruction \cite{park2020nonlocal,yan2022learning,taguchi2023uncertainty}, and self-driving \cite{yan2022desnet,liu2023mff,Zhang2023CompletionFormer}.
elements.id-string-14: In the past few years, plenty of image-guided methods \cite{Cheng2020CSPN,liu2021fcfr,yan2022rignet,lin2022dynamic,Zhang2023CompletionFormer} have been proposed for depth completion under daytime conditions, \emph{e.g.}, the well-known KITTI benchmark \cite{Uhrig2017THREEDV}.
elements.id-string-15: However, there are very few approaches focusing on the more challenging nighttime scenarios.
elements.id-string-16: As we know that nighttime depth-aware self-driving is especially important but difficult.
elements.id-string-17: As shown in Fig.\ref{fig_day_night_comparison}, existing state-of-the-art image-guided depth completion methods \cite{park2020nonlocal,yan2022rignet,Zhang2023CompletionFormer} perform well in daytime conditions but struggle in challenging nighttime scenarios.
elements.id-string-18: This is because the sparse depths from LiDAR are illumination-invariant while the color images are highly affected by visibility and illumination variations.
elements.id-string-19: Therefore, we identify the key challenge of nighttime depth completion as the guidance from color images, which heavily suffer from \emph{poor visibility} and \emph{complex illumination}.

elements.id-string-28: To tackle this issue, we propose \emph{Recurrent Inter-Convolution Differencing} (RICD), which explicitly and gradually estimates global illumination to improve the poor visibility, by using continuous differencing between two convolutions with different kernels.
elements.id-string-29: It is a new perspective to treat the small-kernel-convolution feature as the center of the large-kernel-convolution feature.
elements.id-string-30: Moreover, we recognize that convolution subtraction \cite{shi2022symmetric} is useful for modeling uncertainty \cite{kendall2017uncertainties} where the target pixels are difficult to predict accurately.
elements.id-string-31: In the nighttime image above, we can easily observe that there are many areas with underexposure, overexposure, and terminatorn \footnote{For simplicity, we use '\emph{terminatorn}' to denote the junction area between light and dark.} effects due to varying illumination, resulting in more and higher uncertainty than usual.
elements.id-string-32: Based on these priors, we transform the uncertainty in nighttime scenarios into relative light intensity by applying continuous convolution differencing.
elements.id-string-33: Such differencing features that capture explicit light intensity information are essential for predicting valid illumination.
elements.id-string-34: Consequently, RICD contributes to robust visibility enhancement of nighttime color images with more naturalistic visual effect \footnote{Natural Image Quality Evaluator (NIQE) \cite{mittal2012making}, a completely blind no-reference metric,the lower, the better.} in Fig \ref{fig_color_cast}.
elements.id-string-35: \emph{For complex illumination}: However, even after applying RICD enhancement, the distribution of relative light intensity in nighttime color images is still much more complex than in daytime conditions.
elements.id-string-36: For instance, there are lots of terminatorn areas with varying illumination, which are difficult for standard convolutions to handle.
elements.id-string-37: Fortunately, inspired by the Local Binary Pattern operator \cite{ojala1994performance,boulkenafet2015face} that is robust to illumination variation, a series of central convolution differencing algorithms \cite{yu2020searching,yu2020fas,su2021pixel,tan2022semantic} are devised to address these challenging scenarios.
elements.id-string-38: Nevertheless, their differencing centers are typically fixed, leading to restricted applicability, especially for self-driving where safety is incredibly important.
elements.id-string-39: For example, when the center contains noise or lies on terminatorn, these algorithms would additionally introduce negative reference information, thus resulting in unsatisfactory illumination robustness.
elements.id-string-40: To tackle this issue, we propose \emph{Illumination-Affinitive Intra-Convolution Differencing} (IAICD) that learns reasonable differencing center within a single convolution.
elements.id-string-41: For one thing, IAICD can reduce the latent impact of noise and predict an adaptive differencing center based on the surrounding neighbors.
elements.id-string-42: For another, the estimated illumination map in RICD module is involved to adaptively measure the contribution of every neighbor.
elements.id-string-43: As a result, IAICD could cope with the complex illumination in challenging nighttime scenarios.
elements.id-string-44: Finally, considering the nighttime depth estimation \cite{wang2021regularizing,liu2021self,zheng2023steps} is a highly relevant task, we further evaluate the performance of our model on it.
elements.id-string-45: In summary, our main contributions are as follows:
elements.id-string-47: For the first time, we extend the conventional depth completion task into challenging nighttime environments to compensate for safe self-driving applications.We identify the key challenge of nighttime depth completion as the guidance from color images, where the visibility is low and illumination is complex.
elements.id-string-48: Thus we propose RICD and IAICD with learnable differencing centers, which are rather suitable for nighttime scenarios.We build two benchmark datasets for the nighttime depth completion task.

elements.id-string-140: \textbf{Architecture.} The pipeline of our learnable differencing center network (LDCNet) is illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig_pipeline}.
elements.id-string-141: Overall, LDCNet consists of an image guidance branch and a depth prediction branch.
elements.id-string-142: In the image guidance branch, the low-light image $\boldsymbol x$ is first fed into RICD, generating the enhanced image $\boldsymbol x'$ and the illumination map $\boldsymbol m$.
elements.id-string-143: Next, a simple Unet-like subnetwork $\Phi_c$, composed of five layers with resolutions 1/1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/16, is conducted to encode $\boldsymbol x'$.
elements.id-string-144: Together with $\boldsymbol m$, then the features of each layer are input into IAICD.
elements.id-string-145: In the depth prediction branch, the sparse depth $\boldsymbol d$ is encoded by a similar subnetwork $\Phi_d$.
elements.id-string-146: Meanwhile, the output features of IAICD are resolution-wisely leveraged to guide the dense depth prediction in $\Phi_d$, yielding the final depth output $\boldsymbol o$.

elements.id-string-155: \textbf{RobotCar-Night-DC.} Oxford RobotCar \cite{maddern20171} is a large-scale dataset that captures various weather and traffic conditions along a route in central Oxford.
elements.id-string-156: We create RobotCar-Night-DC from the 2014-12-16-18-44-24 sequences by using the left color images of the front stereo-camera (Bumblebee XB3).
elements.id-string-157: To generate sparse and groundtruth depth maps, we employ the official toolbox to process the data from the front LMS laser and INS sensors.
elements.id-string-158: Following KITTI benchmark \cite{Uhrig2017THREEDV}, we use the current frame for sparse depth generation and multiple frames for groundtruth depth creation.
elements.id-string-159: The densities of the valid pixels of sparse depth and groundtruth depth are about $4\%$ and $16\%$, respectively.
elements.id-string-160: Then we crop and resize these data to $576\times 320$ to remove the car-hood and enable efficient training.
elements.id-string-161: As a result, the RobotCar-Night-DC dataset contains $10,290$ RGB-D pairs for training and $411$ for testing.
elements.id-string-162: \textbf{CARLA-Night-DC.} CARLA-EPE \cite{zheng2023steps} is a synthetic dataset for nighttime depth estimation task using the CARLA simulator \cite{dosovitskiy2017carla} and EPE network \cite{richter2022enhancing}.
elements.id-string-163: The groundtruth depth amps in CARLA-EPE are almost fully dense, which is unrealistic for LiDAR-based self-driving systems that have a groundtruth depth density of around $7\%$ \cite{yan2022rignet}.
elements.id-string-164: Therefore, based on the synthetic dataset we create CARLA-Night-DC for the proposed nighttime depth completion task, by transferring the sparse LiDAR pattern of KITTI \cite{Uhrig2017THREEDV} to CARLA-EPE.
